newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia puts brave face on Lisbon summit isolation.
newsitem.headline: Russia puts brave face on Lisbon summit isolation.

text.p: Russia, putting a brave face on its diplomatic isolation at this week's OSCE summit in Lisbon, on Wednesday hailed the forum as a triumph for its ideas on the future of European security.

Leaders of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) wound up their two-day gathering on Tuesday with calls to respect democracy and human rights and backing for greater arms control.

But they rebuffed Russia's bid to develop the OSCE into a more powerful security body to act as a counterweight to NATO. Western leaders, ignoring Russia's oft-stated concerns, spoke out in favour of NATO's eastward expansion.

Brushing aside these setbacks, the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement: "The main result of the summit is that our idea for creating a new model of European security is winning increasing support.
"In spite of everything our vision of European architecture in the 21st century...is forging its way ahead," it said.
The ministry also lauded an agreement reached at the summit to update the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, an issue Moscow has been pushing since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who led the Russian delegation to Lisbon, sounded a similiarly upbeat note on his return to Moscow on Wednesday.
"I consider that we have executed our task and I am satisfied with the work of the Russian delegation at the OSCE summit," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying.
"The documents which were approved reflect our participation in the forum and make a contribution to the creation of a strong, peaceful and democratic Europe."
Chernomyrdin later briefed President Boris Yeltsin on the summit at the Barvikha sanatorium near Moscow where the Russian leader is recovering from open heart surgery.

"The president believes that there is a basis for the growth of constructive dialogue with many of Russia's partners on questions of European security," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.

In addition to the arms accord, Russia was able to draw comfort from the fact that the forum's final declaration issued no endorsement of NATO enlargement, which Moscow regards as a threat to its own security.
Russian diplomats also succeeded in deleting from the final text a call for greater democracy in Yugoslavia, currently suspended from the OSCE and traditionally supported by Moscow.
Chernomyrdin's determination to keep references to NATO enlargement and Yugoslavia out of the final declaration was partly aimed at disarming his nationalist critics at home, diplomats said.
But despite hard-won concessions in the final declaration, Russia remains in danger of isolation from Western Europe and still seems unsure of its place on the world stage, they added.

Russian support for Yugoslavia's embattled President Slobodan Milosevic and hardline Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko, both accused by opponents of dictatorial tendencies, highlighted the gulf between Moscow and Western leaders.

"The Lisbon summit has stated divisions rather than a convergence of views," said the liberal daily Izvestia on Wednesday. "The NATO eastern express...has already split Europe, leaving Russia in not entirely proud isolation with its sole ally, Belarus."
